title: SAVE America Act Blocked Again in Senate as GOP Tries Reconciliation End Run
excerpt: House Republicans embed voter ID mandates in a $95 billion spending framework, but Republican defections and a hostile Senate Parliamentarian ruling make passage unlikely before the 2026 midterms.
body:
• House Republicans are trying to pass the SAVE America Act through budget reconciliation, bypassing the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold with a $10 billion grant program to incentivize states to adopt voter ID and proof-of-citizenship requirements.
  • The bill has failed twice in the Senate after four Republican senators — Collins, Murkowski, McConnell, and Tillis — joined Democrats to defeat it 48-50.
  • The Senate Parliamentarian has ruled the SAVE Act's provisions do not qualify for reconciliation, and retiring Sen. Thom Tillis has threatened to block any further attempts.
  • For naturalized citizens, including Indian Americans, the bill's documentary proof-of-citizenship requirement could create new barriers to voter registration ahead of the 2026 midterms.

A New Path for a Stalled Bill

House Republicans are making another run at President Donald Trump's signature voting legislation, the SAVE America Act, this time trying to force it through the Senate via budget reconciliation after repeated failures on the chamber floor.

https://x.com/MauckPaul20249/status/2078293588379664459

The House Budget Committee voted 20-14 on Thursday to adopt a $95 billion reconciliation resolution that includes $10 billion in election-related grants over 10 years, according to Democracy Docket. The grants would be conditioned on states adopting voter ID requirements and proof-of-citizenship mandates — the core provisions of the SAVE America Act that the Senate has twice rejected.

"Even if the $10 billion grant program cleared both chambers, it would take effect in Fiscal Year 2027 — too late to change voting rules for this election cycle.</p>"

The Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, as it is formally known, would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, mandate photo identification at the polls, and require states to take additional steps to verify voter eligibility. In its broadest form, the legislation would also ban no-excuse mail voting.

Senate Resistance Runs Deep

The bill's troubles in the Senate are not just procedural — they are political. When Sen. Lindsey Graham offered a SAVE Act amendment during a vote-a-rama in June, it failed 48-50. Four Republicans — Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — voted with every Democrat to block it.

Murkowski has said the bill would set up barriers for voters in her large, rural state. Collins faces a competitive reelection race. McConnell and Tillis, both retiring, have raised concerns about nationalizing election rules that have traditionally been left to states.

"If I see a reconciliation bill come from the House with another failed attempt to confuse this election, I will use every device I have available to slow down the wheels of government until people cop a clue and do the math."

— Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.)

Adding to the bill's problems, the Senate Parliamentarian ruled last month that the SAVE Act's provisions do not have a clear budgetary impact — a requirement for reconciliation bills. Republicans are attempting to sidestep the ruling by restructuring the legislation as conditional grants rather than direct mandates, but budget experts have said that approach is unlikely to survive scrutiny.

Trump's Relentless Push

Trump has made the SAVE Act a central domestic priority. He refused to sign the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in protest over Congress's failure to pass the voting bill, letting it become law without his signature. He used his Independence Day address and a primetime speech on Thursday to demand its passage, claiming — without evidence — that 278,000 noncitizens were registered to vote.

Multiple studies and voter registration audits have found that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare. By some estimates, noncitizen votes account for approximately 0.000007 percent of all ballots cast, according to the Center for American Progress. Voting by noncitizens is already a federal crime punishable by imprisonment and deportation.

What It Means for Indian Americans

For naturalized citizens — a category that includes a large portion of the Indian American population — the bill's documentary proof-of-citizenship requirement could create real obstacles. Not all naturalized citizens have immediate access to their naturalization certificates, and obtaining replacement documents from USCIS can take months. Voting rights advocates have warned that documentary proof requirements would disproportionately burden immigrants who became citizens through the naturalization process.

What Happens Next

The reconciliation resolution's passage on the House floor is far from guaranteed, and its reception in the Senate appears hostile. With Congress set to recess in August and the campaign season consuming October, there are only a few legislative weeks left before the November 2026 midterms. Even if the $10 billion grant program cleared both chambers, it would take effect in Fiscal Year 2027 — too late to change voting rules for this election cycle.
